slides.title: Why do we use Docker?
slides.notes: Spend about 4 minutes. Link back to the different machines on slide 7. Say: Sending the source code alone leaves other people to assemble its environment. An image packages our app with its runtime and libraries so we can start containers from the same package. Docker provides tools to build, distribute and run these packages. Explain consistency, easier setup, isolation and repeatable releases. Containers still require a compatible host and deliberate configuration, credentials and storage. This does not promise identical results from a changing external AI API. Keep this within the existing 09:20–10:05 block by shortening the later recipe recap.
slides.staticHtml:
Package the app with the software it needs, then run that package on a compatible host.

01

A consistent starting point

The app uses the packaged runtime and libraries, rather than whatever happens to be installed on each machine.

02

Less setup to repeat

Build an image once. Other people can start containers from that image without assembling every dependency by hand.

03

Separate app environments

Different apps can use different library versions. Their processes run in isolated environments.

04

Repeatable releases

Test an identified image, then deploy that same package. Keep a known-good version available for recovery.

Docker supplies tools to build, share and run container images.

We still need a compatible host, network, credentials and persistent storage. Containers share the host kernel.

slides.title: Imagine opening a burger stall
slides.notes: Spend about 5 minutes. Say: To make the same burger at another location, a recipe alone is not enough. The other kitchen might lack ingredients or use different equipment. Ask the room what each restaurant item corresponds to in software, then click that row to reveal its match. Reveal rows individually, or use Reveal all. Recipe is application code. Ingredients are libraries and dependencies. Stove and utensils are the runtime and environment. The kitchen is the operating system and server. A packaged food station represents a container. Docker is the system used to create and manage these stations. Clarify the boundary of the analogy: a container uses the host kernel rather than carrying a complete independent operating system. Later, distinguish the reusable station package or blueprint (image) from a running station (container). The example is an analogy, not a claim about how real food businesses operate.

slides.title: The recipe and the image warehouse
slides.notes: Say: The Dockerfile tells Docker how to prepare the application environment. It gives us repeatable build instructions. Consistent results also depend on controlled source, base-image and dependency versions; changing external inputs can change the result even when the Dockerfile stays the same. Once we build an image, a registry stores it so other developers, servers or cloud platforms can download it. Read the examples without ranking them. The registry stores images, not running containers. The image is our prepared packaged meal, and the container is a running serving of that package.

Dockerfile

Tells Docker how to prepare the application environment, giving us repeatable instructions for building an image.

For consistent builds, keep the source, base image and dependency versions controlled.
02 / The warehouse

Registry

Stores the images we build so other developers, servers and cloud platforms can download and run them.

The registry holds images. A server runs containers from those images.

slides.title: The recipe-to-running-app journey
slides.notes: Read the diagram from left to right. Dockerfile is the recipe. docker build prepares the image, our packaged meal. docker push uploads the image to a registry, the warehouse. docker pull downloads the image onto another machine. docker run starts a container from the image, like serving the meal. Pulling does not itself start a container. docker run can automatically pull an image if it is missing locally, but the diagram separates the operations to explain them. A local build and run can skip the registry. Unlike a meal, an image is reusable and can start many containers.

slides.title: Containers and virtual machines
slides.body:
Virtual machine

Includes a guest operating system with its own kernel. A hypervisor provides virtual hardware.

Container

Runs isolated processes that share the container host’s kernel. The image supplies the app’s files.

They often work together: a cloud VM can host containers.
slides.notes: Spend 5 minutes. For Linux containers on macOS or Windows, Docker Desktop commonly uses a Linux VM. Avoid claiming containers are identical to VMs or are an absolute security boundary.

slides.title: The container is running, but the page won’t open
slides.notes: Say: Docker reports that the container is running, but our browser cannot connect to the page. Show the illustrative localhost error. Ask which evidence the audience wants next: published ports and app logs are useful. ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED means the connection attempt was refused, but it does not prove a missing port mapping. The app could also be listening on the wrong address or port, or not be serving requests. The exact browser wording varies. Running is not equivalent to healthy or reachable.
options: B · Check port publishing and the app’s listening address.
slides.answer: B. Check port publishing and the app’s listening address. “Running” does not guarantee browser access. This error is a clue, not proof of one specific cause.

slides.title: A Dockerfile is a packing recipe
slides.notes: Assume no development experience. First click app.py in the file browser: it contains the instructions that make the app work. Click requirements.txt: it lists extra Python software packages the app needs, such as a web framework. It does not contain the company business requirements. Click /app: this is a folder path inside the image/container filesystem, like a folder in a computer, not a website address. / is the root, app is a chosen folder name. WORKDIR /app selects it and creates it if missing. Walk through the four recipe steps. Copying requirements.txt only copies the list. pip install reads the list and installs packages into the Python environment, usually outside /app. COPY app.py . copies the app file into the current working directory. CMD records the startup command; it does not start the app during the build. The simplified recipe omits security and port details covered elsewhere. Production requires reviewed versions and a suitable user. Read no more syntax than the audience needs.

slides.title: Why changing app.py can rebuild faster
slides.notes: Read the Dockerfile from top to bottom. FROM chooses the Python base image. COPY requirements.txt adds the dependency list. RUN pip install installs those packages. COPY . . copies the remaining project files, including app.py. CMD records how a container should start the app. Click Change app.py: with the same base, unchanged requirements and a usable build cache, Docker can reuse the earlier steps and rerun the application copy. Click Change requirements.txt to show that changing an earlier input invalidates that step and the later steps. The four boxes are a simplified explanation: the base image may already contain several layers. CMD is configuration metadata, not a filesystem layer. This sample omits a working directory, a non-root user and other production details to focus on cache ordering. In a real project, use .dockerignore to exclude secrets and unnecessary files. Cached builds do not automatically refresh dependencies.
slides.staticHtml:
Keep the dependency steps before the application files.

Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

CMD records the startup command.
It does not add a filesystem layer.

slides.title: What happens after “Submit feedback”?
slides.notes: Click Submit feedback and then Next step. The browser sends the rating. The app checks the input and asks the database to save it. The database writes its files to a persistent volume; after a successful commit the app can confirm the save. The UI compresses these operations into four teaching steps. Then replace the app container: the stored record remains. Replace the database container: in this example it reconnects to the same volume and reads the record. This assumes a compatible database version and correct mount/configuration. A persistent volume is separate from the container lifecycle but is not a backup. Reset or page refresh clears this browser-only simulation.

slides.notes: Compare the rows after explaining stop versus remove on the previous slide. The writable layer belongs to an individual container and disappears when that container is removed. Clarify that inside the container refers to its logical writable filesystem; the underlying bytes are still stored on the host. slides.title: A standard GitHub Actions workflow
slides.body:
Workflow file: .github/workflows/ci.yml

name: Docker CI
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t ai-app:ci .
      - name: Run tests
        run: docker run --rm ai-app:ci python -m pytest

When it runs

on starts the workflow for a push or pull request.

Where it runs

runs-on selects an Ubuntu runner.

What it does

uses calls an action.
run executes a command.
Steps run in order.

Example assumes the Docker image includes Python, pytest and the test files. This workflow checks the app; deployment comes later.
slides.notes: Walk through the YAML from top to bottom. The name labels the workflow. The on field declares its triggers. permissions grants read access to repository contents. The build-and-test job runs on an Ubuntu runner. Checkout fetches the repository, Docker builds the image, and pytest runs inside a temporary container. A failing build prevents the test step from running by default. The example assumes a Dockerfile at the repository root and an image containing Python, pytest and the tests, with no incompatible ENTRYPOINT. Use mocked model responses for predictable tests. YAML indentation defines structure. This is an illustrative CI workflow, not a production deployment pipeline. Source: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax
